stemMd: In paragraph 2, the author says that a trader who returns to the same pitch every week "is playing a long game". As used in the passage, this phrase means that the trader:
instructionsMd: Answer on the basis of the passage only.

options.label: A
options.textMd: acts with an eye to the benefits of many future dealings rather than to immediate gain.

options.label: B
options.textMd: deliberately delays replacing faulty goods until customers stop complaining.

options.label: C
options.textMd: competes against the other traders in a contest that lasts the whole season.

options.label: D
options.textMd: spends many hours at the market on each Saturday.

options.label: E
options.textMd: takes large risks in the hope of a single large reward.

explanationMd:
An idiom is defined by what the author says next. The sentences after "playing a long game" contrast "a few euros today" with customers who will not come back, and then say that "the value of a good name is the stream of future sales it protects". The "long game" is therefore one in which the trader gives up a small gain now to keep a larger stream of sales over many future Saturdays.

**Check:** "long" here refers to the time horizon of the trader's interests, not to the length of a market day or of a competition. Substitute the meaning into the sentence and the rest of the paragraph follows from it.

distractorRationale.d: This reads "long" as the length of a working day. The passage's next sentences are about future weeks and future customers, not about hours spent at the stall.
distractorRationale.b: The passage says traders replace faulty goods "without argument". Delaying replacements is the opposite of the behaviour the phrase is used to explain.
distractorRationale.e: A single large reward is what cheating would offer, and the passage says such a gain is worth far less than the stream of future sales. The phrase describes patience, not gambling.
distractorRationale.c: This takes "game" literally as a contest between traders. The passage is about a trader's relationship with customers over time, and rivalry between traders is never mentioned.
